# Norway slams brakes on AI data center boom over grid fears 

Statnett pauses new data center approvals through July 2027 as it develops safeguards for large, fast-changing power loads.

 Published Nov. 13, 2026 

 

 Shane Snider Senior Reporter, Infrastructure 

 

 The Northern Lights carbon capture and storage facilities owned by Equinor, Shell and TotalEnergies on Dec. 16, 2024, near Bergen, Norway. Getty Images 

Norway’s transmission operator has frozen new grid-capacity reservations for data centers and certain other large electricity consumers while it develops technical requirements to protect the power system from sudden demand changes.

Statnett announced the temporary suspension on Monday. It expects the pause to last no later than Aug. 1, 2027. The measure covers new capacity reservations and certain applications for technical approval, including projects with unusual load profiles that could affect grid operations.

The decision comes as Statnett tracks 32.1 GW of data center capacity across different stages of development: 800 MW already connected, 4,200 MW with capacity reserved, 9,100 MW in the connection queue and another 18,000 MW in additional connection requests.

Those figures do not represent committed construction or electricity demand that the grid must serve immediately. They do, however, show the scale of interest in a country whose peak electricity demand has only slightly exceeded 25 GW.

The Norwegian data center industry said the suspension creates uncertainty for projects already under development, including some that have secured grid capacity but still need technical approval.

“Projects in the queue will have to wait for a grid-capacity reservation. Projects that already have reserved capacity could also face delays if they still need a technical approval covered by the suspension,” said Reynir Johannesson, managing director of Norwegian Data Center Industry, a trade group.

The suspension also affects Norwegian contractors and suppliers, who need to plan staffing, procurement and future work, Johannesson said. The association is asking Statnett to clarify how it will handle pending applications, which projects can proceed, and when applicants can expect decisions.

Statnett is using the pause to develop requirements for how large computing facilities behave during grid disturbances and how quickly they change their electricity consumption.

“This is a risk-reducing measure for the power system,” said Siri Gjørtz, Statnett’s press chief. The suspension will remain in place while the operator develops the knowledge base needed to establish future requirements.

Statnett has not identified a specific disturbance caused by a Norwegian data center. A government-commissioned report from Menon Economics also cautioned that, although grid-stability problems have emerged elsewhere, Norway has not yet established whether the same requirements apply to its power system.

### Statnett targets load behavior

The technical work will address how data centers respond to disturbances, including whether they remain connected when grid conditions deteriorate. Statnett also wants to manage rapid changes in electricity consumption and reduce the risk that large computing loads trigger oscillations.

Those concerns reflect the operating characteristics of some AI facilities. Training workloads can produce recurring changes in power demand, while protection systems and uninterruptible power supplies can disconnect or reconnect substantial loads during electrical disturbances.

Menon’s report noted that Norway’s hydropower-heavy grid has considerable inertia and that data center demand has historically represented a limited share of the country’s electricity use. The report said further work is needed to establish whether technical requirements developed in other countries would apply in Norway.

The Norwegian Data Center Industry said it supports efforts to protect grid stability, but wants Statnett to develop requirements in consultation with operators.

“We take grid stability seriously. The Norwegian Data Center Industry is ready to work with Statnett on clear, measurable requirements that are proportionate to each facility’s impact on the power system,” Johannesson said.

Those requirements could cover how facilities respond to grid disturbances and how quickly they change their power consumption, he said. Developers need clear standards before they design facilities, while operators need a way to demonstrate compliance.

Ireland provides a documented example of the operational risk. On June 6, a single-phase fault at the Poolbeg 220-kV substation caused about 480 MW of data center demand to disconnect, representing about 52% of total data center demand at the time, according to grid operator EirGrid.

EirGrid maintained system security during the event. Its modeling also found that as much as 90% of data center demand could disconnect under certain credible three-phase faults.

The June event followed earlier large data center disconnections in Ireland. EirGrid has been examining grid-code requirements for fault ride-through, active-power recovery and the rate at which facilities change their electricity consumption.

“We’re seeing a wave of data center regulations and grid connections reforms in Europe,” said Paweł Czyżak, founder of Ornaq, an independent AI and energy think tank. He cited grid-connection reforms in Spain, Portugal, Denmark, Finland, the United Kingdom and Poland.

“In most cases, the data center-related challenges in Europe were more administrative – blocking grid capacity and making grid planning difficult,” Czyżak said. “Going forward, and given the scale of the buildout in countries like Norway or Finland, the challenges might become technical: grid balancing, ensuring a supply surplus, grid stability.”

Denmark also pauses connections

Norway is not the first European country to suspend new grid connections amid a surge in large-load requests.

Denmark’s transmission operator, Energinet, paused new grid-connection agreements in March after receiving requests for about 33.5 GW of new transmission-connected consumption. Those requests covered data centers, power-to-X projects and battery facilities, not just data centers.

The volume dwarfed Denmark’s peak electricity demand of roughly 7 GW. Energinet has since moved away from a first-come, first-served approach toward screening projects based on their maturity.

The pauses reflect a growing problem for grid planners: developers can reserve or request capacity years before they build facilities or secure customers. Those requests can complicate transmission planning and block capacity that other projects may need.

Neil Osnato of Persistence Analytics Group said grid planners should not treat capacity reservations as proof that a project will proceed.

“A megawatt requested, a megawatt reserved, a megawatt deliverable and a megawatt generating sustained revenue are not interchangeable,” Osnato said.

He argued that developers should demonstrate site control, financial commitments, customer demand and progress against milestones before holding scarce grid capacity. Without those checks, utilities risk building infrastructure for projects that stall, shrink or never materialize.

### Government plans licensing system

The grid pause coincides with a broader Norwegian government effort to control data center development.

On Monday, the government proposed a licensing system for existing and future data centers. It wants to prioritize facilities it considers socially beneficial, including those supporting defense, emergency preparedness, healthcare, digital security and computing capacity for Norway and Europe.

The proposal would exclude cryptocurrency mining from that category. The government also wants developers to contribute more toward grid expansion and operating costs and is examining ways to encourage new electricity generation, including offshore wind and gas power with carbon capture and storage.

The government has not enacted the licensing system. It plans to establish its main principles in autumn 2027 and develop transitional arrangements.

The Norwegian Data Center Industry challenged the premise that data centers lack societal value, arguing that facilities provide digital infrastructure for businesses, public services and individuals through cloud services, secure data storage and computing for research, industry and AI.

The association considers cryptocurrency mining an exception. “Cryptocurrency mining in itself should not qualify a facility for priority,” Johannesson said.

If the government prioritizes projects based on societal value, the criteria must be transparent and verifiable, he said. The government also needs to explain how a licensing system would treat existing grid-capacity reservations, investments already made and contracts already signed.

Johannesson warned that uncertainty over connection dates could affect investment decisions. “If investors and customers do not have a grid connection date they can plan around, some may defer investment or choose another country.”

He said clear technical requirements developed with industry and aligned across countries could help other European markets. But he was skeptical that Norway’s broader approach would become a template: “Whether Norway’s broader approach becomes a model for Europe? Don’t count on it.”

The proposed rules would add a second layer of scrutiny beyond Statnett’s technical requirements: whether a data center should receive permission to operate in Norway at all.

### Existing projects keep their place

Statnett’s suspension does not cancel existing connections or automatically remove projects already in the queue. Facilities with the required technical approvals can proceed, and the operator will continue processing certain pending applications, particularly projects expected to enter service soon and those connecting through regional distribution networks.

Applications involving direct connections to the 420-kV transmission grid also fall under the suspension.

Statnett said the pause will not allow other customers to move ahead of data center projects that have already progressed further through the connection process.
